24 hours vs 48 hours: the notice window is a waitlist question

Trainers, salons, and tutors search this because a client who wants a shorter cancellation window will argue that 24 hours is “industry standard.” Booking software exposes both toggles. None of them tell you how much of the empty-chair hole a longer rule actually closes.

The fee is not the refill. Charging 100% of the session price still leaves the hour unsold unless someone from the waitlist takes it. A same-day cancel is almost never refillable. A 48-hour cancel often is — if you keep a list and actually call it.

On a typical $75 session, 20 bookings a week, and an 8% late-cancel rate, those openings are $6,240 of chair time a year. If you refill 10% same-day, 40% with 24 hours, and 65% with 48 hours:

NoticeAssumed fillCash recoveredStill emptyExtra vs same-day
Same day (4 hours)10%$624$5,616$0
24 hours40%$2,496$3,744$1,872
48 hours65%$4,056$2,184$3,432

The extra $3,432 is not a promise. It is what happens if you can actually hit 65% fill with two days of notice. If your waitlist is empty at every window, a 48-hour rule recovers nothing extra.

Open the no-show fee calculator, enter your price, weekly bookings, no-show rate, and the fill rates you have actually seen. It shows the empty-slot cash recovered at 4 hours, 24 hours, and 48 hours next to the fee-level table. Nothing is uploaded.

This page is arithmetic, not legal or business advice. It does not tell you which policy to publish. Confirm what your payment processor and local rules allow before you send a number to clients.

Common questions

Is a 48-hour cancellation policy better than 24 hours?

Only if you actually refill more cancelled slots with the extra day. A longer notice window that does not change your waitlist fill rate is just a longer argument with the client. Compare your own fill rates on the same booking volume.

Does a no-show fee replace a waitlist?

No. A collected fee compensates for holding the slot. It does not put another client in the chair. The empty-slot cash and the fee are separate numbers.

No-Show & Cancellation Fee Calculator

For personal trainers, salons, tutors, therapists, and other appointment-based service businesses: put a specific, defensible number on your no-show fee and get a policy you can hand to clients today.

After using this, you can now state and defend a specific no-show/late-cancellation fee — and hand clients a ready-to-use policy — which used to take guessing a number or copying a boilerplate template that doesn't match your prices.

Already booking through scheduling software? This calculator vs. Acuity Scheduling explains why the two sit next to each other: the platform carries and enforces the policy, this page works out the number that goes in it.

Pricing an upfront deposit instead of an after-the-fact fee? The appointment deposit calculator turns your service price into a deposit amount, balance due, and draft policy — nothing uploaded.

Tempted to just pick a round number? Why a flat fee guess doesn't scale with your price shows what a flat $25 guess costs a $200 session versus a $35 one.

Your numbers

No conversion is performed. Choose the currency your prices already use.

Not sure? Count last month's no-shows and late cancels, divide by total bookings, times 100.

Compared against chasing the no-show fee after the fact. The deposit is treated as already collected when the slot is reserved — not as a second invoice you have to chase.

What one overflow hour costs you: overtime, a voucher, a refund, or lost goodwill. Leave blank to price it as one full session. Used only in the overbooking table.

Waitlist fill if you get that notice (your assumption)

How often you actually refill a cancelled slot when the client gives you that much warning. Same-day is usually near zero; 48 hours is why people ask for it. Count last month's late cancels that you filled, or leave the defaults. Why 24 hours vs 48 hours is a cash question.

This only changes the draft wording. Confirm your payment processor and booking-system rules before using it.

"Revenue those slots represent" is the value of the appointments themselves — the fee does not replace that lost service time, it compensates for holding the slot. "Estimated fee revenue" uses your assumed enforcement rate above and is a model, not a promise. Missed-slot revenue recovered compares that modeled fee revenue with the value of the missed appointments. The break-even count is the number of fully collected fees needed to cover that annual exposure; it is not a target or a guarantee. Modeled annual exposure still unrecovered is the same comparison stated as a full-year dollar figure rather than a monthly slice, clamped at zero. None of these figures predict client behavior or guarantee collection.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a no-show or late cancellation?

There's no single right number, but a common starting point is charging close to the full service price for a true no-show (the slot usually can't be rebooked) and a partial fee for a late cancellation with some notice. This calculator turns your own price, notice window, and fee percentage into a specific number.

Is a cancellation or no-show fee legal?

Charging a disclosed cancellation fee is common practice across many service industries and is generally enforceable when clients agree to it in advance, but rules vary by location, payment processor, and industry — some regions treat fees for medical or dental appointments differently, for example. This is not legal advice; check the requirements for your business type and location.

How much notice should I require?

24 hours is the most common default — usually enough time to fill the slot from a waitlist. Businesses with longer or harder-to-fill sessions often use 48 hours instead. The table above compares same-day, 24-hour, and 48-hour windows using your own fill-rate assumption so you can see how much empty-slot cash a longer window actually recovers.

Should I overbook or charge a no-show fee?

They recover different money. A fee pays you when the chair stays empty and you collect. Overbooking tries to fill that chair in advance and risks a double-booked hour when everyone shows. The table above compares a fee-only book to overbooking 50%, 100%, and 150% of your expected no-shows, plus matching the rate and dropping the fee. It does not tell you which policy to publish.

Should I take a deposit instead of charging a no-show fee?

A deposit is collected when the client books, so a late cancel does not depend on a second collection attempt. A no-show fee is invoiced after the missed slot, so it only comes in at the rate you actually enforce. Compare the two on your own numbers above — this tool does not decide which is lawful or appropriate for your business.

Usage

Everything above runs in your browser. Nothing you type is ever uploaded — there is no server, no account, and no analytics vendor. This calculator counts a small number of anonymous events (which buttons were used, nothing about who used them) and keeps the count only in this browser, so it can tell whether anyone is using it at all. Your calculator numbers are also saved locally for convenience and can be removed with Reset saved numbers.

should-i-overbook-or-charge-a-no-show-fe.text:
← No-show & cancellation fee calculator

Should I overbook or charge a no-show fee?

Trainers, salons, tutors, and therapists search this after a week of empty chairs. A booking app will toggle a fee. A colleague will say “just book one extra.” Those are different recoveries. The fee pays you when the chair stays empty and you actually collect. Overbooking tries to fill the chair in advance and risks a double-booked hour when everyone shows.

Open the no-show calculator, keep your own price and no-show rate, and optionally type what a collided chair costs you. The table below uses the page defaults: $75 a session, 20 bookings a week, 8% no-shows (1.6 empty chairs), a 100% fee collected 70% of the time, and overflow priced as one full session.

The fee-only book, then matching the empty chairs

Book only the 20 chairs and 18.4 of them sit. Service for the year is $71,760. The 83.2 no-shows, charged at $75 and collected 70% of the time, add $4,368. Net kept: $76,128.

Put 1.6 extra names on the same book — matching the no-shows you already expect. Expected arrivals rise to 19.872. Nobody overflows on the mean. Service rises to $77,500.80 and the larger book still generates $4,717.44 of fee revenue. Net kept: $82,218.24, which is $6,090.24 more than the fee alone.

Drop the fee and only overbook those 1.6 names and you keep $77,500.80. That still beats the fee-only book. It does not beat filling the chairs and collecting on the names that still miss.

Policy Extra / week Overflow / week Net kept / year vs fee only
Capacity only, collect fee0.00.00$76,128.00$0.00
Overbook 50% of expected no-shows + fee0.80.00$79,173.12$3,045.12
Overbook 100% of expected no-shows + fee1.60.00$82,218.24$6,090.24
Overbook 150% of expected no-shows + fee2.40.61$80,520.96$4,392.96
Overbook to match, drop the fee1.60.00$77,500.80$1,372.80

When the extra name starts to cost you

Booking 150% of expected no-shows fills every chair on the mean (20.0 served) but overflows 0.608 chairs a week. At $75 per collision that is $2,371.20 a year, and the net falls to $80,520.96 — still above the fee-only book, below matching the rate. Price overflow at $0 and the aggressive book wins, because the extra fees are then free. A medical chair or a one-person studio often prices overflow above one session; type that number.

This is a mean-value model. A week whose average fits can still collide on a high-show day. The overflow cost is how that risk is priced, not a promise that 1.6 extra names never double-book. Rates are yours. The page does not tell you to overbook, to charge, or that a fee is lawful in your location.

Common questions

Should I overbook or charge a no-show fee?

They recover different money. On the calculator example — a $75 session, 20 bookings a week, an 8% no-show rate, a 100% fee collected 70% of the time, and overflow priced as one session — booking only the chairs you have keeps $76,128 a year. Overbooking to match the 1.6 expected empty chairs and still collecting the fee keeps $82,218.24, which is $6,090.24 more. Dropping the fee and only overbooking keeps $77,500.80.

When does overbooking cost more than a no-show fee?

When extra names push expected arrivals past capacity and a collided chair is expensive. On the same example, booking 150% of expected no-shows serves every chair but overflows 0.608 chairs a week. At $75 per collision that costs $2,371.20 a year and the net falls to $80,520.96 — still above the fee-only book, below matching the rate. Price overflow at $0 and the aggressive book wins because the extra fees are free.

Does a no-show fee replace the lost session?

No. The fee compensates you for holding the slot. The service revenue only counts chairs that were actually sat. That is why a collected fee and a filled chair are not the same dollar, and why the calculator shows both lines.

vs-a-flat-no-show-fee.html.text:
← No-show fee calculator

No-Show Fee Calculator vs. guessing a flat dollar fee

Guessing a flat fee is the default method, because it needs no calculator: pick a round number that sounds reasonable — $20, $25, $50 — and charge it for every no-show, whatever the missed appointment was worth. It works for exactly the services priced near that number. It stops working the moment your price list spans more than one tier, because a flat number carries no information about what any specific session costs — a $200 session and a $35 session lose it at the same rate.

Same flat guess, two real price points, both running the same 50%-of-price policy this calculator would compute.
BusinessPriceCalculator's fee (50% of price)Flat $25 guessWhat the flat guess gets wrong
Studio Radiance (massage)$200$100.00$2512.5% of the session — too little to matter against a $200 loss
Fresh Cuts (barbershop)$35$17.50$2571% of the ticket — a steep fee for a $35 service

Both businesses picked the same policy — half the session price — and the calculator prices it at $100 for the massage studio and $17.50 for the barbershop, because it starts from each business's own price. A flat $25 guess starts from neither: it is barely an eighth of what the massage studio's own policy says a no-show costs, and nearly three-quarters of the barbershop's entire ticket. The same number is simultaneously too small and too large, because it was never priced against either service to begin with. At its own volume (60 bookings a week, a 12% no-show rate), the barbershop's annual exposure is $13,104 — a real number a flat guess never engages with either way, since it happens to sit close to that business's own 50%-of-price fee only by coincidence of the ticket size chosen for this example.

Studio Radiance50%-of-price feeFlat $25 guess
Fee per no-show$100.00$25.00
No-shows per year (25 bookings/wk, 8% rate)104
Annual exposure (slots at risk, unenforced)$20,800.00
Estimated annual fee revenue at 70% enforcement$7,280.00$1,820.00
Estimated share of exposure recovered35%8.75%

The gap is $5,460 a year, and it has nothing to do with how well the fee is enforced — both columns assume the identical 70% enforcement rate. It is entirely the fee amount: $25 was never priced against a $200 session, so collecting it every time still leaves most of the exposure on the table. Figures from this calculator's own computeFeeAmount, computeAnnualExposure, and computeAnnualFeeRevenue, run on the inputs in this table.

Common questions

What's wrong with just picking a round number like $25?

Nothing, at the one price where $25 happens to be the fee you would have calculated anyway. Below that price it charges more than your own policy would justify; above it, it charges too little to matter. A flat number doesn't know what your service costs, so it can only be right by coincidence.

Can you show it with real numbers?

A $200 massage session and a $35 haircut both run a 50%-of-price cancellation policy. The calculator prices that at $100 for the massage and $17.50 for the haircut — each half the session's own value. A flat $25 guess charges 12.5% of the massage price (too little to offset a $200 loss) and 71% of the haircut price (an aggressive fee for a $35 service). Same guessed number, opposite problem at each end.

Does the gap actually add up to real money?

At 25 bookings a week, an 8% no-show rate, and 70% enforcement, the massage studio's own 50%-of-price policy collects an estimated $7,280 a year against $20,800 of exposure. The same no-shows billed at a flat $25 collect an estimated $1,820 — $5,460 a year left uncollected, not because enforcement failed but because the fee itself was priced for a cheaper service.

Is a price-proportional fee always the right call?

Not automatically — a percentage that feels fair for one service can feel steep for another even at the same price, and this tool does not know your local market or client relationships. What it does is show you the actual dollar consequence of the percentage you pick, at your own price, instead of leaving you to guess a flat number that was never priced against your service at all.

Open the no-show fee calculator and enter your own price to see the fee your policy actually implies, not a number borrowed from a different business's price list.

vs-acuity-scheduling.html.text:
← No-show fee calculator

This calculator vs. Acuity Scheduling

Different jobs: one holds the appointment, the other decides what the missed appointment is worth.

Acuity Scheduling is a well-known appointment-scheduling platform, described on acuityscheduling.com — a booking page clients use themselves, calendar sync, automated reminders, intake forms, and, through a connected payment processor, collecting payment when someone books. It is the kind of tool a trainer, salon, tutor or therapist runs their whole diary through, and the place a cancellation policy is shown to clients when they book.

That is a different job from the one this page does. This calculator has no booking page, no calendar, no client records and no account. It exists for the step that comes before you fill in any of those settings: turning your session price, weekly bookings, no-show rate, notice window and honest waitlist refill rate into a specific fee, an estimate of what the empty slots cost you over a year, and a policy paragraph you can paste into whichever booking system you already use.

What each tool answers

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
What should the fee actually be, given my price, my no-show rate, and how often I refill the slot? This calculator — it returns a specific number and shows the annual exposure behind it.
Is 24 hours or 48 hours of notice worth more to me? This calculator — the notice-window page prices the extra day against your own waitlist fill rate.
Would overbooking the empty chairs keep more than collecting the fee? This calculator — the overbooking page compares the two on the same book.
Where do clients book, get reminders, and see the policy before they agree to it? A scheduling platform such as Acuity Scheduling — booking pages, reminders and enforcement are jobs this page does not attempt.
How do I take the money, at booking or afterwards? Your scheduling platform and its connected payment processor. This calculator only models which of the two keeps more.
Is the fee lawful and allowed by my processor where I trade? Neither. That is a question for your own advisers and your processor's terms, and no calculator settles it.

The same split applies whatever you book through. Calendly, Mindbody, Square Appointments, Vagaro and a paper diary are all places a policy can live; none of them is where the number comes from. If you already pay for scheduling software, keep it — this page is not an alternative to it, and switching is not the point.

What this page deliberately does not tell you: what any of these platforms cost, which plan includes which setting, or how their cancellation options are configured. Those change, and a stale figure repeated here would mislead you. Check each platform's own site for that, and check this calculator for the number you are going to type in.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Acuity Scheduling?

Both, for different jobs. Acuity Scheduling is an appointment-scheduling platform: a booking page clients use themselves, calendar sync, automated reminders, intake forms, and, through a connected payment processor, collecting payment when someone books. This page is none of that. It has no booking page, no calendar, no client list and no account. It answers the one question a scheduling platform asks you rather than answers: what number should the fee be. Put your session price, weekly bookings, no-show rate, notice window and honest waitlist refill rate in, and it returns a specific fee, what the empty slots cost you over a year, and a policy paragraph you can paste into whichever booking system you already use.

Where does the number in a cancellation policy come from?

From you. A cancellation setting in any booking system is a field: a percentage or amount, and how much notice a client has to give. The software then carries that policy and applies it the same way every time, which is genuinely the hard part of collecting anything. What it cannot do is know your refill rate, so the number itself is still yours to decide. That is the gap this calculator fills, and it is why the two sit next to each other rather than competing.

Is this page affiliated with Acuity Scheduling?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Acuity Scheduling or Squarespace, and it is not affiliated with any other booking platform named on this page. Those names appear only to describe what this calculator is and is not. Each is a trademark of its respective owner. Check any platform's own site for what its current plans and settings actually include, because this page deliberately publishes none of their prices or feature details.
